turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in, both of you. The nurse left a note about wheezing after a cold, but I want to hear it myself. What's been the main trouble?

[SEG0002] person_2 (CAREGIVER): I'll jump in. I'm his mom, and he gets formal and undersells it. He's been tight and wheezy for ten days, ever since that cold hit, and he was up all night barely breathing.

[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Thank you, but I need to correct that. The cold began about ten days ago, mostly a runny nose, and that has cleared. The wheezing has been five days, not ten. I did sleep, just not well, and I would not say I was barely breathing.

[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): All right. So the cold is about ten days, and the wheeze is either five or ten depending on which of you I ask. I'll keep it as roughly five to ten days and not pretend we pinned the day. Marcus, what does it actually feel like?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): It is a whistling in my chest when I breathe out. I get short of breath if I lie flat, so I have been sleeping in the recliner, which helps.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is there a cough with that?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Yes. A dry cough, worse at night. It wakes me once or twice.
[SEG0008] person_2 (CAREGIVER): And the inhalers. I lose track of which color is which, and so does he. He has been on one of them constantly.

[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): I use the blue one when I wheeze. I thought it was four times a day, but counting yesterday, it was maybe five, six times a day, two puffs each time. I do mix the blue and the brown up when I am tired.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Five or six times a day of a rescue inhaler is a lot. I'm thinking the airways are still irritable after that cold. What is the blue one, exactly, and what is the brown?

[SEG0011] person_2 (CAREGIVER): Blue is albuterol. Brown is Flovent, fluticasone, the one hundred ten microgram one... no, sorry, they switched him to the two hundred twenty. Two puffs twice a day is the plan, though he barely touches the brown one.
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): I would not say barely. I use the brown inhaler most mornings, two puffs. I often skip the evening dose. That part is fair.

[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, partial use, not zero. So albuterol, the ninety microgram inhaler, two puffs, five or six times a day lately. Fluticasone two hundred twenty, two puffs prescribed twice a day, mostly mornings. Did I hear that right?
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): Yes, Doctor. That is correct.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever with this?
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): No. I have not had a fever.
[SEG0017] person_2 (CAREGIVER): I put a hand on his forehead last night. It was cool.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest pain? Any blood when you cough?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): Neither. No chest pain, and I am not coughing up blood.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): How about your stomach, with the coughing at night?
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): My stomach is fine. No nausea.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or vape?
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): No. I have never smoked.
[SEG0024] person_2 (CAREGIVER): He's home from college for the month, which is why I'm hovering. His father has asthma too, the same sort of wheeze.
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): I have had asthma since I was seven. It stays quiet when I keep up with the brown inhaler. I am studying history, if that matters, which it likely does not.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any medicine that gives you a rash, swelling, or trouble breathing?
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): No. I have no known drug allergies.
[SEG0028] person_2 (CAREGIVER): Nothing I have ever seen, either.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Before you sat down the nurse ran a peak flow. I nearly wrote three hundred ten, but her figures say three hundred forty liters per minute. Scratch the three ten.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): She also got a pulse of ninety-two and an oxygen saturation of ninety-seven percent on room air. You're speaking in full sentences, which I find reassuring.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me listen. There is a wheeze on both sides, mostly when you breathe out. I do not hear crackles, and you are not pulling at your neck. No real distress.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): It eases a little more when I sit up like this. Thank you for talking it through.

[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm putting this together as an asthma flare set off by the cold. The wheeze, what I hear, and how fast you're going through albuterol all fit. I don't see pneumonia here, no fever and no crackles, though a plain post-viral twitch of the airways is still on the list.
[SEG0034] person_2 (CAREGIVER): They gave him steroid pills once back in high school. Are we doing that again?

[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. I was about to say prednisone forty milligrams once a day for five days. Actually, with this much rescue inhaler use, I'll make it fifty milligrams by mouth, once a day, for five days.
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Fifty milligrams, not forty. Should I take it with food?
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): With breakfast, so it is easier on your stomach. Finish all five days even if you feel well on day two.

[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): The blue albuterol stays the rescue, two puffs when you wheeze, but five or six times a day is a warning, not a habit. The brown fluticasone, two hundred twenty, is two puffs every morning and every evening, including days you feel fine. You had the jobs of those two switched in your head.
[SEG0039] person_3 (PATIENT): I did. Blue when I wheeze, brown every morning and every night. I will try not to skip the evening dose.
[SEG0040] person_2 (CAREGIVER): I'll tape a label on each canister tonight so neither of us has to guess by color.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Please do that. I don't want a chest x-ray today. If the wheeze hasn't settled after the steroid course, we might get one.
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): What should I watch for in the meantime, Doctor?
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you can't finish a sentence, if your lips look blue, or if the albuterol isn't touching the wheeze, go to the emergency room. Don't wait that out until morning.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): I also want to see you back here in five days, after the prednisone, and we'll repeat the peak flow.
[SEG0045] person_3 (PATIENT): Five days is acceptable. I have a seminar, though I can move it.
[SEG0046] person_2 (CAREGIVER): He will talk your ear off about that seminar if you let him. We'll be here.
[SEG0047] person_3 (PATIENT): It is only a discussion section on the New Deal. My breathing comes first. I apologize for wandering off.

[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): No need to apologize. One gap I won't paper over is that I don't have your personal best peak flow, so three forty is just a number today, not a percentage. I'm treating what I see, not a percent predicted.
[SEG0049] person_3 (PATIENT): I do not remember a personal best either. I am sorry I cannot supply it.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then it stays unknown, and that's all right. If you have a spacer, use it on both inhalers, slow breath in, hold it about ten seconds.
[SEG0051] person_2 (CAREGIVER): The spacer is in the hall closet, behind the winter coats. I'll dig it out tonight.
[SEG0052] person_3 (PATIENT): I will use it. May I confirm the prednisone, so I do not mishear? Is fifty milligrams the final dose?
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Final answer is fifty milligrams once a day for five days. Forget the forty. That was me thinking aloud and then correcting myself.
[SEG0054] person_2 (CAREGIVER): I'll nudge him at night about the brown inhaler. He is very polite in here and then he gets lost in a book.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): That nudge matters, because I'm not convinced the twice-a-day fluticasone is really happening. Mornings, yes. Evenings, we just don't know.
[SEG0056] person_3 (PATIENT): That is fair. I cannot say the evening doses have been consistent.
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): Reception can book you on the way out, five days from today. If you are clearly worse before then, don't wait for that visit.
[SEG0058] person_3 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate that you explained your reasoning rather than only handing me a prescription.

omissions.text: Orthopnea detail: shortness of breath occurs when lying flat, and he has been sleeping in a recliner because it helps.
Dry cough is worse at night.
Patient often skips the evening dose of fluticasone and uses it mostly in the morning; medication record says 'currently used' twice daily without this key adherence detail.
Negative finding: no vomiting was reported in addition to no nausea ('stomach is fine').
Negative finding: patient denied vaping as well as smoking; only never-smoked status is explicitly captured.
Exam detail: no accessory muscle use/retractions at the neck ('not pulling at your neck').
Assessment detail: doctor felt pneumonia was unlikely because there was no fever and no crackles.
Doctor explicitly decided not to order a chest x-ray today; only the conditional future x-ray is recorded.
Follow-up plan includes repeating the peak flow at the five-day return visit.
Clinical uncertainty: doctor does not know the patient's personal best peak flow, so 340 L/min could not be interpreted as a percentage.
